aristotle-practical-wisdom: Aristotle held that being good is not just following rules but knowing how to act well in particular situations. Practical wisdom (his word is phronesis) is the developed ability to see what a situation really demands and to weigh competing goods — honesty against kindness, courage against caution. On this view it is a skill of judgment built through practice, not something a rulebook can supply.
brain-in-a-vat: The brain in a vat is a modern skeptical scenario: a brain removed from its body is kept alive in a tank and fed electrical signals by a computer. Everything it experiences feels exactly like a normal life, yet none of it is real. Since, skeptics argue, your experiences could be like that too, you could never be certain the world around you exists.
cartesian-doubt: In his Meditations, Descartes proposed doubting everything that could possibly be doubted, as a method for finding something certain. The senses sometimes mislead, dreams can feel like waking life, and perhaps a powerful deceiver tricks us even about simple truths. What survives, he argued, is his own existence as a thinking thing — 'I think, therefore I am.' It remains the classic opening move of modern debates about knowledge.
cartesian-dualism: Descartes argued that reality contains two different kinds of thing: minds, whose essence is thinking, and bodies, which occupy space and obey physical laws. On this view you are essentially a thinking mind attached to, but distinct from, your body. A famous objection is how the two could interact — how an immaterial mind moves an arm or feels a stubbed toe — so many philosophers have doubted the split.
commodity-fetishism: Marx observed that in a market economy, products seem to have value and a life of their own, as if a car were expensive simply because it is a car. He called this commodity fetishism: the human labor and social relations behind a product disappear behind its price, so we end up relating to each other through things, and things seem to rule us.
eliminative-materialism: Eliminative materialism is the radical view that our everyday way of describing minds — in terms of beliefs, desires, and choices — is a primitive folk theory that neuroscience may turn out to be wrong about, the way alchemy was abandoned. If so, these concepts would not be refined but eliminated and replaced by brain science. Many find this too strong, but it poses how much common sense must survive.
experience-machine: Philosopher Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could give you any experiences you wanted, all perfectly pleasurable and indistinguishable from real life. If pleasure were all that mattered for a good life, we should plug in. Most people hesitate, and Nozick took this to show we value actually doing things, being a certain kind of person, and living in contact with reality — not just having pleasant experiences.
fate-vs-free-will: If a higher being already knows everything you will ever do, can your choices still be free? Knowing what someone will do seems different from making them do it, so many philosophers — following Boethius — argue that seeing the future, even infallibly, compels no one. Others reply that a fully fixed future leaves no genuine room for choice. The puzzle remains one of the oldest challenges to free will.
free-will-determinism: Determinism is the idea that every event, including every human action, is fully brought about by prior causes, so that given the past and the laws of nature, only one future is possible. If that is true, it is unclear whether we genuinely choose or merely feel that we do. Many hold that freedom is compatible with determinism if it means acting from your own desires; others disagree.
ghost-in-the-machine: The ghost in the machine is Gilbert Ryle's mocking name for the picture, associated with Descartes, of the mind as a hidden inner self piloting the body. Ryle argued this rests on a category mistake — treating the mind as one more thing alongside the body, when mental life is just what living bodies do. The phrase survives as shorthand for any imagined inner controller behind outward behavior.
hard-problem: Neuroscience can explain how the brain processes information, directs attention, and triggers behavior — David Chalmers calls these the 'easy' problems. The hard problem is why any of this is accompanied by subjective experience: why there is something it feels like to see red or feel pain, rather than everything happening 'in the dark.' No agreed explanation exists, and many hold it may force a rethink of the physical world.
higher-lower-pleasures: John Stuart Mill argued that pleasures differ not only in amount but in quality: pleasures of the mind — thought, art, friendship — are higher than merely bodily ones. His test was the verdict of those who have experienced both, and he claimed such 'competent judges' would not trade a higher pleasure for any quantity of the lower. Critics ask whether this escapes hedonism or only refines it.
hume-bundle: When David Hume looked inside his own mind, he could find only particular perceptions — sensations, thoughts, feelings — succeeding one another, never a self that has them. He concluded there is no simple, persisting ego, just a 'bundle' of perceptions bound together by memory and resemblance. Many find this unsettling but honest; others argue the unity of consciousness points to something more than a bundle.
intentionality: In philosophy, intentionality is the 'aboutness' of the mind: beliefs, hopes, fears, and perceptions are always about something — the cup, the meeting, the person you miss. Franz Brentano took this directedness as the mark of the mental, since a mere physical thing seems to be about nothing. Phenomenologists such as Husserl built on the idea, studying how the world is given to consciousness through perceiving, remembering, and imagining.
knowledge-argument: Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who knows every physical fact about color vision but has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room. When she first sees a red tomato, does she learn something new — what red looks like? If so, complete physical knowledge leaves something out, the standard argument that conscious experience is more than the physical. Whether Mary really learns anything new is still debated.
marx-ideology: For Marx, the ruling ideas of an age tend to be the ideas of its ruling class: beliefs that make the existing order — its property, power, and inequalities — seem natural, fair, or inevitable. Ideology works through what he called false consciousness, where people absorb a picture of the world that serves their masters' interests against their own. None of it need be deliberate; the system generates the illusions.
philosophy-of-humor: Why do we laugh, and what makes something funny? Three classic theories compete: humor as felt superiority, humor as the delight of perceiving an incongruity that suddenly snaps into sense, and humor as the release of nervous tension. Philosophers also ask whether jokes can be morally judged — whether laughing at a cruel joke makes you complicit in it — and many hold that it can.
plato-euthyphro: In Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, Socrates asks: is something good because the gods approve it, or do the gods approve it because it is good? Either answer is troubling — if approval makes things good, morality is arbitrary, while if the gods recognize goodness already, it exists independently of them. The dilemma still shapes debates over whether morality needs religion.
punishment-theory: What justifies punishing people? Retributivists hold that wrongdoers deserve to suffer for their crimes, and that this desert is itself the reason to punish. Rehabilitation focuses instead on reforming offenders so they can rejoin society, while deterrence aims at preventing future crime. The views pull in different directions — retribution can demand suffering with no benefit, rehabilitation may understate desert — and most real systems try to combine them.
skepticism: Philosophical skepticism is the challenge that we may know far less than we assume — perhaps nothing about the external world, other minds, or even our own past. Ancient Pyrrhonians recommended suspending judgment altogether, while Descartes used doubt as a tool to hunt for certainty. Few accept the most extreme conclusions, but skeptics force other philosophers to show what actually justifies our confidence in ordinary knowledge.
socratic-method: The Socratic method, or elenchus, is a form of questioning in which one person, feigning ignorance, draws out another's beliefs and exposes their contradictions until a more defensible position emerges. Socrates used it in the Athenian marketplace to test claims about justice, courage, and the good life — often to the embarrassment of the confident. It survives in law schools and classrooms as learning by structured question and answer.
virtue-ethics: Virtue ethics, in the tradition of Aristotle, focuses on character rather than rules or consequences: the central question is not 'what should I do?' but 'what kind of person should I be?' Virtues — honesty, courage, generosity — are stable traits built through habituation, and acting well means acting as a practically wise, flourishing person would. Critics note it offers less guidance; defenders reply real situations rarely allow it anyway.
web-of-belief: W. V. O. Quine proposed that our beliefs face experience not one by one but as a connected web. When observation clashes with what we expect, no single belief is forced to go: we may adjust a peripheral belief, or even a central one about logic, wherever the web absorbs the blow most cheaply. This holism helps explain why reasonable people can react to the same evidence differently.
what-is-it-like: Thomas Nagel argued that a creature is conscious when there is 'something it is like' to be it — a subjective feel from the inside. Even a complete physical account of a bat's sonar system, he claimed, would not tell us what it is like for the bat to experience the world. Objective, third-person facts seem to leave out the first-person point of view, so consciousness resists standard methods.
